results.title: Leveraging Static Analysis for Feedback-Driven Security Patching in LLM-Generated Code
results.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable potential for automatic code generation. Yet, these models share a weakness with their human counterparts: inadvertently generating code with security vulnerabilities that could allow unauthorized attackers to access sensitive data or systems. In this work, we propose Feedback-Driven Security Patching (FDSP), wherein LLMs automatically refine vulnerable generated code. The key to our approach is a unique framework that leverages automatic static code analysis to enable the LLM to create and implement potential solutions to code vulnerabilities. Further, we curate a novel benchmark, PythonSecurityEval, that can accelerate progress in the field of code generation by covering diverse, real-world applications, including databases, websites, and operating systems. Our proposed FDSP approach achieves the strongest improvements, reducing vulnerabilities by up to 33% when evaluated with Bandit and 12% with CodeQL and outperforming baseline refinement methods.

results.title: Static Analysis-Guided Patch Synthesis for Correcting LLM-Generated Insecure Code
results.abstract: Abstract LLMs often miss subtle security conditions such as boundary checks and authentication flows. We introduce a static-analysis-driven patch synthesizer that transforms insecure LLM output into correct and safe code. The pipeline uses abstract interpretation to detect violations, followed by SMT-guided repair rules. On 3,200 vulnerable code snippets across five vulnerability categories, our system achieves 74% full automatic repair and 92% partial repair, outperforming Codex and GPT-4 post-processing by a large margin. Developer usability evaluation shows 58% reduction in manual fix time. The method highlights how program analysis can systematically strengthen LLM-based secure coding.

results.title: Efficiency Analysis of LLM-generated Dynamic Programming Code: A Benchmarking Study using EffiBench Framework
results.abstract: The widespread availability of LLMs has shown their capabilities in helping developers with automated code generation. In contrast, a number of studies have verified the accuracy of LLM-generated codes [2], [4], but little research has been done on code efficiency, in particular [8], [10]. The efficiency of GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-mini, GPT-5.4-nano and GPT-4-turbo-four LLMs operating on LeetCode dynamic programming problems, is analysed in this paper [10]. I evaluate the codes on six metrics like Execution Time(ET), Max Memory Usage(MU), Total Memory Usage(TMU),Normalized Execution time (NET), Normalized Max Memory Usage (NMU) and Normalized Total Memory Usage (NTMU) on 277 dynamic programming problems using EffiBench framework [10]. The performance of humanwritten canonical solutions taken from the LeetCode repository has served as the basis for standardizing all metrics. The GPT-5.4 mini model has the best efficiency profile with a mean NET of 1.20, NMU of 1.06, and NTMU of 1.52, while the GPT-4turbo model has the highest resource consumption with a NET of 1.93, NMU of 1.26, and NTMU of 2.84. The results highlight the need to evaluate LLM-generated code based on efficiency, which is particularly important for dynamic programming algorithms [8], [11]. This research provides empirical data on the performance of recent LLMs in producing code for complicated algorithmic problems [13], pointing out the tradeoffs involved in the generation process with reference to model size, execution time, and memory consumption.

results.title: A Systematic Literature Review of Traditional and LLM Approaches to Static Code Analysis for Bug Detection
results.abstract: Static bug detection plays an important role in software development, serving to preemptively identify potential coding errors and vulnerabilities before running the program. In this sense, static bug detection provides the advantage of not requiring a programmer to execute their code constantly to discover errors. As such, the vast majority of software ecosystems utilized for software development employ static bug detection techniques. This paper evaluates multiple static bug detection tools across various software ecosystems, seeking to explore the differences and effectiveness of such tools. More specifically, within the realm of static bug detection, we consider two main approaches: traditional (non-machine learning) methods, and Large Language Model (LLM) based methods. We evaluate multiple static bug detection tools within each of these two categories by performing a literature review of relevant works, focusing on a sample of 11 relevant literature that explores tools and approaches from the traditional category and the LLM category.
